title: Growing Food in the City
passage:
Walk through almost any large city today and you may notice something unexpected: tomatoes growing on a balcony, herbs in a window box, or rows of beans on the roof of an office block. Urban gardening, the growing of plants for food in towns and cities, has become popular around the world. This is surprising, because cities have very little free land, and most of it is expensive. Yet millions of people have found ways to grow food in small, unusual spaces.

The idea is not new. During the First and Second World Wars, many governments asked citizens to grow vegetables in parks and back gardens so that farms could send more food to the army. These plots were often called victory gardens. After the wars ended, however, supermarkets became cheaper and more convenient, and interest in home growing fell. It returned in the 1970s, when rising food prices made people look for cheaper ways to feed their families, and it has continued to grow ever since.

One of the main attractions of urban gardening is the quality of the food. Vegetables picked a few minutes before a meal taste better than those that have travelled long distances, and gardeners know exactly what has been used to grow them. Several studies suggest that people who grow their own vegetables tend to eat more of them, which can improve their diet. Children seem to benefit especially: pupils who help to grow salad leaves at school are often more willing to try them. There are also small savings, as a packet of seeds costs far less than the same amount of food in a shop.

Gardening can also bring people together. In community gardens, a group of neighbours shares a piece of land and divides the work. Newcomers to a city, who may know nobody, often say that these gardens are where they made their first friends. Older people who live alone find a reason to go outside, and younger volunteers learn practical skills from them. Some gardens hold weekly meals using the harvest, and extra vegetables are frequently given to local food banks. In this way, a small plot can become the centre of a neighbourhood.

Plants also help the city itself. Concrete and metal absorb heat, so central districts are often several degrees warmer than the countryside. A layer of plants on a roof keeps the building below cooler in summer, which reduces the need for air conditioning. Soil and leaves soak up rainwater, lowering the risk of flooding in heavy storms. Flowering plants provide food for bees and butterflies, and these insects are becoming scarce in many cities. Even a few pots on a balcony can make a difference when many households do the same.

Urban gardening does have difficulties. Soil in older cities may contain metals from past industry or traffic, and eating vegetables grown in it could be unsafe. Experts therefore advise gardeners to test the soil first, or to plant in raised beds filled with clean earth. Tall buildings may block sunlight, so gardeners must choose plants such as lettuce that tolerate shade. Water can also be costly, although collecting rain from roofs solves part of this problem. With careful planning, most of these obstacles can be overcome.

title: The Story of the Pencil
passage:
The pencil is one of the most ordinary objects in the world. Millions of them sit in school bags and kitchen drawers, and few people stop to ask where they came from. Yet the story of the pencil includes a lucky accident, a guarded mine, and a clever solution to a wartime shortage. Before pencils existed, writers used pens dipped in ink, or thin sticks of lead that left only a faint grey mark on paper.

The key material, graphite, was discovered in the 1560s in Borrowdale, in northern England, after a storm pulled a large tree out of the ground and revealed a black substance beneath its roots. Local shepherds soon used it to mark their sheep. Graphite proved useful for other jobs as well; it was used to line the moulds in which metal cannonballs were made. Because pure graphite is soft and dirty to hold, early users wrapped it in string or a piece of sheepskin.

A better solution came from Italy, where craftsmen are believed to have made the first wooden pencils by cutting a groove in a stick, placing a thin piece of graphite inside, and gluing the halves together. The idea spread across Europe, and demand grew quickly. The English mine was valuable, so it was guarded, and it was opened for only a few weeks each year. Pencil makers in other countries often struggled to find enough graphite.

The shortage became serious in France in the 1790s, when war with Britain stopped imports. In 1795 a French inventor, Nicolas-Jacques Conté, found a way to make pencils without pure graphite. He ground low-quality graphite into powder, mixed it with clay, shaped the mixture into thin rods, and baked them in an oven. This gave makers control: with more clay the pencil became harder, and with less clay it became softer. Pure graphite pencils had always been equally soft, so Conté's method allowed writers and artists to choose between light and dark lines for the first time.

Erasers arrived more slowly. For many years people rubbed out mistakes with small pieces of bread. In the 1770s it was noticed that a piece of natural rubber could remove pencil marks, which is why the material is still called a rubber in British English. In 1858 an American, Hymen Lipman, received a patent for a pencil with an eraser fixed to one end by a small metal band, known as a ferrule. The design is still seen everywhere today.

Today, billions of pencils are produced every year. Many are made from cedar wood, which is easy to sharpen and does not split easily. Most are hexagonal, a shape that is comfortable to hold and stops the pencil from rolling off a desk. Although computers and phones have replaced pencils for many tasks, they remain popular with artists, builders, and students, partly because they need no battery and rarely break.

title: The Clever Crow
passage:
Crows are often seen as ordinary city birds, picking at rubbish or calling noisily from rooftops. Scientists, however, have come to regard them as some of the cleverest animals on Earth. Crows belong to a group of birds called corvids, which also includes ravens and jays. Compared with the size of their bodies, corvid brains are large, and in some respects their behaviour resembles that of apes. This is one reason researchers study them so closely.

The best-known example of this intelligence is tool use. New Caledonian crows, which live on a small island in the Pacific, make tools from twigs and the edges of leaves. They shape a twig into a hook and use it to pull insects out of holes in dead wood, a task their beaks cannot manage. Young birds watch adults at work and gradually copy them, so different groups develop slightly different designs.

Laboratory experiments have confirmed these skills. In one test, a crow was given a piece of straight wire and a small bucket of food at the bottom of a tube. The bird bent the wire into a hook and lifted the bucket out, although it had never seen wire before. In another test, based on an old story, crows dropped stones into a tube of water to raise the level and reach a floating treat. The birds chose large stones over small ones, which showed they understood which would work better.

Crows also take advantage of human cities. In parts of Japan, they have been seen placing hard nuts on roads so that passing cars crack the shells. The birds then wait for traffic lights to turn red and hurry across to collect the food safely. Nobody taught them this method; it seems that one crow discovered it and others learnt by watching. This shows how quickly crows can adapt to new surroundings.

Another remarkable ability is memory for faces. In one study in the United States, researchers wearing a rubber mask caught and released several crows. Years later, the birds still scolded anyone who wore that mask, but ignored people in other masks. Even more surprising, crows that had not been present at the original event also reacted angrily, which suggests that the information had been passed on.

The social lives of crows are complex. They often live in family groups, and young birds may stay with their parents for several years to help raise the next generation of chicks. When a crow dies, others gather around the body and call loudly. Researchers think this behaviour may help them learn about possible danger. These discoveries interest scientists because bird brains are built very differently from those of mammals, so the cleverness of crows suggests that intelligence can develop in more than one way.

title: Walking: The Simplest Exercise
passage:
Few forms of exercise are as simple as walking. It needs no special equipment, no membership of a gym, and no particular skill. Yet in many countries people walk far less than they did a generation ago, because of cars, lifts, and jobs that involve sitting at a desk for hours. Doctors are now encouraging patients of all ages to build more walking into their daily routine, and many people measure their progress using phone apps or small devices that count steps.

The popular goal of 10,000 steps a day has an unusual history. It first appeared in Japan in the 1960s, when a company selling a step-counting device gave it a name that means 10,000 steps meter. The number was an advertising slogan rather than the result of scientific research. Since then it has spread worldwide and is now built into most fitness watches. Recent studies, however, suggest that the main health benefits begin at much lower totals, and that for many adults the extra steps beyond seven or eight thousand add only a little.

The physical benefits of regular walking are well documented. It strengthens the heart and helps to keep blood pressure at a healthy level. Walking also uses the muscles and bones of the legs, which slows the loss of bone strength that comes with age. Because it puts less stress on the joints than running, it is suitable for people who are overweight or recovering from injury. Many doctors also recommend a short walk after meals to help the body control blood sugar.

Walking is good for the mind as well. Many people find that a walk outdoors lowers stress and improves their mood, especially when it takes place in a park or among trees. Researchers have also found that people who walk regularly tend to fall asleep more easily and wake less often during the night. Some writers and scientists say that they solve problems more easily while walking, and a number of companies now hold short meetings on foot.

The difficulty for most people is not knowing that walking is useful but turning it into a habit. Experts suggest linking it to something you already do, such as walking part of the way to work or taking a short stroll after dinner. Setting a small, fixed goal is more effective than making vague promises. Walking with a friend or joining a group also helps, as the other person expects you to turn up. Keeping a simple record of your walks can be motivating, too.

Beginners should start gently. Comfortable shoes with good support are the only essential item, since painful feet quickly end a new habit. Rather than attempting a long distance on the first day, add a few minutes to your walk each week and increase the pace gradually. People who have heart problems or other medical conditions should speak to their doctor before starting a new programme. Finally, remember that any walking is better than none: even ten minutes is a worthwhile beginning.

title: The Psychology of Habit
passage:
Every morning, before most of us are fully awake, a chain of actions unfolds with almost no conscious thought: switching off the alarm, walking to the bathroom, reaching for the toothbrush. Psychologists call such actions habits, and they are far more common than we tend to assume. Wendy Wood, a professor of psychology at the University of Southern California, has led diary studies in which volunteers recorded what they were doing and thinking at random moments of the day. Her team concluded that around 43 per cent of everyday behaviour was repeated in the same place almost daily, and that people were often thinking about something else while they did it.

The idea is not new. In 1890 the American philosopher and psychologist William James described human life as "a mere bundle of habits", but for much of the twentieth century the mechanism behind them remained a mystery. The breakthrough came from neuroscience. In the 1990s, Ann Graybiel and her colleagues at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology implanted tiny electrodes in rats that were learning to run a maze for a chocolate reward. At first, the animals' brains were highly active throughout the task. As the route became familiar, however, activity in a deep region called the basal ganglia dropped, apart from sharp bursts at the beginning and the end. Graybiel called this process "chunking": the brain compresses a sequence of separate decisions into a single automatic unit, freeing capacity for other tasks.

What starts a habit and keeps it going? The journalist Charles Duhigg popularised a three-part "habit loop" made up of a cue, a routine and a reward. Research by Wolfram Schultz at the University of Cambridge helps explain why the loop is so powerful. Schultz recorded the activity of dopamine-producing neurons in monkeys that were given drops of juice. At first, the neurons fired when the juice arrived. After repeated trials, however, they fired when a light signalling the juice appeared, and hardly at all when the juice itself was delivered. The brain, it seems, learns to crave the reward in advance. This anticipation produces the urge that pushes us toward the routine, which is why the smell of coffee can feel almost as compelling as the drink.

Cues are frequently tied to a particular setting, and this makes habits surprisingly fragile in new surroundings. Wood and her colleagues studied students who transferred to a different university. Those who had previously read a newspaper, exercised at a gym or watched television as a matter of routine often abandoned these activities after the move, because the familiar triggers had disappeared. Students whose new environment contained the same cues, in contrast, tended to keep their habits. The researchers also found that when a habit was strong, people's stated intentions had little effect on what they did. A student who said she no longer wanted to watch television would still switch it on if she was sitting on the same sofa at the same time of the evening.

Many popular books claim that a new habit takes 21 days to form. The figure appears to originate in the 1960s observations of a plastic surgeon, Maxwell Maltz, who noted that his patients took about three weeks to adjust to their new appearance; it was never tested as a rule for behaviour. When Phillippa Lally and colleagues at University College London did test habit formation in 2009, they asked 96 volunteers to adopt a simple new behaviour, such as eating a piece of fruit with lunch, and to report daily how automatic it felt. The average time needed to reach a plateau of automaticity was 66 days, but individuals ranged from 18 to 254 days. Missing a single day did not significantly reduce the chances of success, which suggests that occasional lapses need not be a cause for despair.

If habits cannot be willed into existence quickly, can they be designed? Peter Gollwitzer, a psychologist at New York University, has spent decades studying "implementation intentions", which are plans written in the form "If situation X arises, then I will do Y". By linking an intended action to a specific cue, such plans effectively create a habit-like trigger in advance. In one of his experiments, participants who wrote an if-then plan stating when and where they would exercise were considerably more likely to follow through than those who merely stated a goal. Other researchers recommend adding friction to unwanted habits, for example by storing snacks out of sight, so that the cue is weakened before the routine begins.

Habit research is not without its critics. Some psychologists argue that the habit loop is too simple to describe complex human behaviour, much of which involves flexible goals and deliberate choices. Others point out that most laboratory findings come from small samples in wealthy countries and may not hold elsewhere. Wood accepts that habits are only one influence among several, yet she maintains that they explain why good intentions so often fail. Understanding the contexts in which our routines unfold, she argues, is more useful than relying on willpower alone.

title: Rebuilding the Reef
passage:
Coral reefs occupy less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species and protect millions of people from storm waves. They are also in serious trouble. Surveys of the Caribbean suggest that the region lost around 80 per cent of its living coral cover between the 1970s and the early 2000s, a decline driven by disease, pollution and overfishing. Since then, marine heatwaves have triggered repeated mass bleaching, a process in which stressed corals expel the algae that give them colour and most of their food. Given losses on this scale, it is hardly surprising that scientists have moved beyond protecting reefs and started to rebuild them.

The most widespread technique is coral gardening. The Coral Restoration Foundation, a non-profit organisation based in Florida, hangs small fragments of staghorn and elkhorn coral from underwater frames shaped like trees, where they grow in clean, well-lit water. When the fragments have matured, divers attach them to damaged reefs. The foundation has planted many tens of thousands of corals this way, and some of them have since spawned naturally. Gardening is valuable, but it cannot succeed alone. Because the nursery colonies are produced by cutting, the planted corals are genetic copies of a few parents, and a single disease outbreak could therefore wipe out an entire plot.

A different approach concentrates on speed. Dr David Vaughan, a marine biologist at the Mote Marine Laboratory in Florida, discovered by accident that when slow-growing brain and boulder corals were broken into pieces about a square centimetre in size, the fragments grew many times faster than intact colonies, and neighbouring pieces fused into a single colony. Species that normally need decades to reach a useful size could reach it within a few years. This "micro-fragmentation" is a genuinely promising technique, although it remains labour-intensive, since every piece must be cut, nurtured and fixed in place by hand.

Fragments, however, can never replace sexual reproduction. Once a year, many corals release eggs and sperm in a synchronised mass spawning, and the resulting larvae are genetically unique. SECORE International, a partnership of aquariums and universities, collects spawn from wild colonies, rears the larvae in tanks, and settles them on small ceramic tiles that are placed on reefs. This produces the genetic variety that fragmenting lacks. The drawback is mortality: the vast majority of the young corals die within months of being placed, so the method relies on producing very large numbers of them.

Others are working on the heat itself. At the Australian Institute of Marine Science, Professor Madeleine van Oppen leads research into "assisted evolution". Her team exposes the microscopic algae that live inside corals to high temperatures for several years, selecting the strains that survive, and then introduces them to young corals. Early laboratory results suggest that corals carrying these strains endure warmer water for longer. Critics warn that releasing modified organisms could have unforeseen effects on natural ecosystems, and that laboratory success may not carry over to the open sea. Such caution is justified, and the field has so far moved slowly.

The most forceful sceptic is Professor Terry Hughes of James Cook University, who documented how two successive marine heatwaves, in 2016 and 2017, killed roughly half of the shallow-water corals on the Great Barrier Reef. Hughes accepts that restoration can help a small site, but points out that the reef system stretches for more than 2,000 kilometres, and that even the most ambitious nursery covers an area that is tiny by comparison. Without sharp cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, he argues, whatever is planted today will simply bleach again. It is hard to dispute his arithmetic.

None of this means that restoration should be abandoned. Local projects can protect a reef on which tourists, fishers and coastal villages depend, and they buy time while governments decide how far to cut emissions. They also train a generation of practitioners and generate knowledge, for instance about which species are most resilient. The sensible conclusion is that reef restoration and emission reduction are complementary rather than competing strategies. Rebuilding corals without slowing climate change is like mopping a floor while the tap is still running; turning off the tap without mopping leaves the floor wet for years.

title: The Economics of Working from Home
passage:
Before 2020, working from home was a marginal activity. Surveys in the United States suggested that fewer than five per cent of paid working days were spent at home, and most employers regarded the practice as a perk granted to a favoured few. The pandemic transformed this almost overnight. According to the economists Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom and Steven Davis, who have tracked the habits of tens of thousands of American workers since 2020, the share of days worked from home rose sharply and then settled at around 28 per cent, about five times the pre-pandemic level. Economists suddenly found themselves studying the largest unplanned experiment in working practice in history.

The best evidence comes from earlier, deliberately designed experiments. In 2013, Nicholas Bloom, an economist at Stanford University, worked with Ctrip, a Chinese travel company, to test home working among its call-centre employees in Shanghai. Of those who volunteered, half were chosen by lottery to work from home for nine months, while the rest stayed in the office. The results surprised many managers. Performance among the home workers was 13 per cent higher. About two thirds of the gain came from employees working more minutes of their shift, since they took fewer breaks and sick days, and the remainder from handling more calls per minute in a quieter setting. The company also found that the rate at which employees left their jobs fell by about half.

Why should working at home pay? For employees, the most obvious gain is time. The average American commuter spends the best part of an hour travelling to and from work each day, and removing the journey returns that time to the worker, part of which is usually devoted to the job itself. Employers, meanwhile, can economise on premises: a company that lets half of its staff work at home several days a week can reduce the amount of office space it leases, and the saving may well exceed the cost of equipping staff at home. In the Ctrip trial, savings on space were a large part of the overall benefit to the company.

There are costs, however, and some are hard to see. The same Ctrip employees who flourished at home were promoted far less often than comparable colleagues in the office, even when their performance ratings were equal, suggesting that managers notice the people they see. Evidence from within a large technology company points the same way. A study of Microsoft employees, led by Longqi Yang and published in 2022, found that when staff began working remotely, their networks of contacts became more tightly clustered inside their own teams, and communication between different teams declined. Such links are often the source of new ideas.

Cities may feel the effects most. Economists such as Edward Glaeser of Harvard University have long argued that cities are productive because proximity helps ideas spread: ambitious people learn from one another in corridors, cafes and meetings. Glaeser doubts that video calls can fully replace this contact. Meanwhile, the geography of cities is already shifting. Two researchers, Arjun Ramani and Nicholas Bloom, have documented a "donut effect" in American metropolitan areas, in which demand for homes and shops has dropped in the centre while rising in outer suburbs. The sandwich shops, cafes and dry cleaners that once depended on the lunchtime crowds of downtown workers have been among the first casualties.

Many firms now hope that a hybrid pattern can keep the benefits and avoid the costs. In 2022, Bloom and colleagues ran a second randomised trial, this time with some 1,600 graduate employees at the same company, who worked at home on two days a week. After two years, their performance and their promotion rates were no different from those of colleagues who attended the office every day. The researchers concluded that hybrid arrangements may be a safer compromise than fully remote work, but they added that the result might not hold in other industries, where output is harder to measure.

Whatever the arrangement, the benefits are unevenly shared. Jonathan Dingel and Brent Neiman, economists at the University of Chicago, estimated that only about 37 per cent of jobs in the United States could be performed entirely at home, and that these were concentrated among higher-paid occupations such as finance and management. Cleaners, drivers and nurses cannot log in from their kitchens. If remote work continues to raise the productivity and the wellbeing of the better paid, it may widen the gap between them and everyone else, which makes the distribution of its gains as important a policy question as its overall size.

title: A Short History of Mapmaking
passage:
The earliest surviving map of the known world is a small Babylonian clay tablet, dating from around 600 BCE. It shows Babylon as a rectangle near the centre, ringed by a circular ocean, with distant regions drawn as triangles beyond the water. Nobody could have used it to travel anywhere; it expressed a belief about where humanity stood in the cosmos. Not every early map was so symbolic. Egyptian surveyors drew plans of farmland so that boundaries could be restored after the annual flooding of the Nile. From the outset, then, maps served two quite different masters: the imagination and the practical needs of property.

Greek scholars brought mathematics to the problem. In the second century CE, Claudius Ptolemy compiled his Geography, a guide that listed the positions of roughly 8,000 places by latitude and longitude and explained how to project a curved globe on to a flat sheet. The work was extraordinarily influential, but it had flaws. Ptolemy had never visited most of the places he described and depended on itineraries supplied by merchants and soldiers, whose estimates of distance were often little more than guesses. He also adopted a figure for the size of the Earth that was too small, which made Europe and Asia appear to stretch much further around the globe than they do. Centuries later this error encouraged explorers to believe that Asia could be reached by sailing west.

After the fall of Rome, Ptolemy's text was preserved and studied in the Islamic world. In 1154 the geographer al-Idrisi completed a world map for King Roger II of Sicily, drawing on the reports of travellers and sailors as well as on earlier Greek and Arabic sources. Al-Idrisi interviewed visitors to Roger's court and compared their accounts, discarding those that contradicted one another, an early example of cross-checking evidence. His map, drawn with south at the top, was probably the most accurate depiction of the Eurasian landmass for the following three centuries, and its influence can be traced in European atlases well into the Renaissance.

The great voyages of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries created a demand for charts that sailors could follow. In 1569 the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator published a world map on a new projection in which lines of constant compass bearing appeared as straight lines. A navigator could therefore draw a single line between two ports and sail along it by holding the same heading. The price of this convenience was distortion: areas far from the equator were stretched, so that Greenland seemed as large as Africa, although Africa is in fact about fourteen times bigger. Mercator's projection nevertheless became standard for marine navigation and, later, for school wall maps.

Knowing where one is at sea, however, required longitude, and for centuries no reliable method existed. After several shipwrecks, the British government passed the Longitude Act in 1714, offering a substantial prize for a solution. The clockmaker John Harrison eventually produced a marine chronometer that kept accurate time through months of rough voyages; by comparing local noon with the time at a home port, sailors could calculate their position east or west. On land, meanwhile, the Cassini family of astronomers spent much of the eighteenth century using triangulation, the measurement of angles between distant landmarks, to map France. Their results revealed that the true coastline lay further inland than earlier maps had suggested.

The twentieth century changed mapmaking again. Aircraft carried cameras above battlefields during the First World War, and by mid-century photographs allowed entire regions to be charted in months rather than decades. Satellites then moved the camera into orbit: the American Landsat programme began imaging the Earth in 1972, and the Global Positioning System, completed in the 1990s, gave anyone with a receiver an exact location. Not everyone welcomed the old projections. In 1973 the German historian Arno Peters campaigned for an equal-area map that showed poorer countries at their true size, arguing that Mercator's image had encouraged Europeans to overestimate their own importance. Many professional cartographers rejected his claims, partly because his map distorted shapes, yet the dispute made people aware that every map is a choice.

Today, digital tools have shifted the power to draw maps. OpenStreetMap, founded by Steve Coast in 2004, is edited by volunteers in much the same way as an online encyclopedia. After the 2010 earthquake in Haiti, thousands of volunteers around the world traced roads and damaged buildings from satellite images within days, giving rescue teams a detailed map of a place that had previously been poorly charted. Critics warn, though, that commercial platforms decide what appears on screen and which businesses are highlighted. The history of mapmaking suggests that this should not surprise us: maps have never been neutral pictures of the world, but arguments about it.

title: The Origins of Language: A Sudden Leap or a Long Road?
passage:
Few questions in the human sciences have proved as resistant to evidence as the one concerning how language began. In 1866 the Linguistic Society of Paris famously banned papers on the subject, judging it unanswerable, and for much of the following century many scholars respected the spirit of that ban. Spoken words leave no fossils, and the oldest written records already display grammar as sophisticated as that of any modern tongue. Since the 1990s, however, the topic has regained respectability, thanks to advances in genetics, comparative primatology and computer modelling. The renewed debate has not produced consensus. Instead, it has sharpened a disagreement over whether language arrived gradually or all at once.

The case for a sudden origin is most closely associated with the linguist Tomasz Wieland. He argues that the essence of language is neither vocabulary nor sound but a single computational operation that combines small units into hierarchically structured expressions of unlimited length. Such an operation, he contends, is an all-or-nothing capacity: a creature either possesses it or does not. Wieland therefore proposes that it appeared through a minor neural rewiring in one population of Homo sapiens perhaps 100,000 years ago, and that speech itself was a later adaptation which merely exploited the new faculty for communication. On this view, asking how language evolved gradually is as misguided as asking how a circuit could be partly switched on.

Wieland's critics find this picture implausibly tidy. The primatologist Helena Marsh points out that non-human primates already display many of the cognitive ingredients that language requires: they track complex social relationships, interpret one another's intentions and, in captivity, can learn hundreds of symbols. Marsh favours a gradualist account in which gesture came first. Great apes, she observes, use manual gestures flexibly and deliberately, whereas their vocal calls are largely involuntary and tied to emotional states. A gestural system could therefore have grown steadily more elaborate before shifting to the voice, a transition that would have been encouraged as hands became occupied with tools and with the carrying of infants.

A third school locates the origin of language in social pressure rather than cognition. The evolutionary anthropologist Amara Okonkwo notes that as early human groups grew larger, the time required for physical grooming, the primate method of maintaining alliances, would have become unsustainable. Language, she proposes, emerged as a cheaper substitute, a form of grooming at a distance that allowed an individual to nurture several relationships simultaneously. Gossip, rather than instructions for hunting, was thus the first great use of speech. The theory is attractive, but it explains why language was valuable without explaining how its grammatical structure arose, a limitation that Wieland is quick to exploit.

Archaeology offers indirect evidence, though it has not settled matters. Kenji Ashworth, who studies stone-tool technology, argues that making the finest hand axes, more than a million years ago, demanded sequences of actions too intricate to be learned by observation alone. In his teaching experiments, novices who received spoken instruction produced serviceable tools far faster than those who merely watched a demonstration. Ashworth takes this as a sign that language, or something close to it, was already in use among toolmakers. Sceptics reply that the experiments demonstrate only that speech can assist learning; they cannot show that it was available to the toolmakers in question.

Genetics has proved similarly equivocal. Mutations in a gene called FOXP2 cause severe difficulties with speech and grammar, and it was once hailed as the language gene, an overstated label. The human variant has since been identified in Neanderthal DNA, which suggests that it predates our species, and most researchers now regard it as one of many genes contributing to the fine motor control of speech rather than as a switch that created grammar. Wieland has responded that this finding concerns only the physical production of sounds, which he considers peripheral, and leaves his claim about the underlying combinatorial operation untouched.

Computer simulation and laboratory experiments have lent support to a different possibility: that structure can emerge without any biological leap. The cognitive scientist Linnea Hartmann asks volunteers to learn an invented language and then pass it on to the next person, forming chains of learners. Because each learner's memory is imperfect, the language is subtly distorted at every stage, and over many generations the distortions accumulate into something remarkably orderly. Initially random vocabularies become steadily more regular, with words built from reusable parts. Nobody intends this result; it arises from the pressures of transmission itself. Wieland counters that the volunteers already possess the relevant capacity, so the experiments cannot show where it came from.

Part of the disagreement may be definitional. If language is understood narrowly as syntax, a sudden origin looks more plausible; if it is understood broadly as communication, gradual accounts gain strength. A growing number of researchers favour a hybrid, in which a long period of biological preparation, including gesture, social cognition and vocal control, was followed by a rapid phase of cultural elaboration. What unites the participants is a recognition that no single discipline can settle the question alone. Whether it will ever be answered is uncertain; at least it is no longer taboo.

title: Resurrecting the Lost: The Ethics of De-extinction
passage:
Early this century, researchers announced plans to revive the passenger pigeon, a bird hunted to extinction a hundred years earlier. Similar ambitions now surround the woolly mammoth and the Tasmanian thylacine. The term de-extinction is something of a misnomer, since no technique can recreate a vanished species exactly. The methods under discussion include cloning from preserved cells, selective back-breeding of living relatives, and genome editing, in which fragments of DNA recovered from museum specimens are inserted into the cells of a close living species. The result would be an animal resembling the lost one, not the lost one itself. Yet even this limited prospect has divided conservationists and ethicists, and the arguments reveal much about how we think about nature.

Supporters stress the practical benefits. The conservation biologist Ingrid Solheim argues that de-extinction should be judged less by its headline species than by the tools it develops. Many endangered populations, such as the black-footed ferret, have lost so much genetic variety that they are vulnerable to disease. Techniques for reading old DNA and editing living cells could restore some of that lost variety, using material from preserved specimens of the same species. Solheim therefore regards the revival of extinct animals as a by-product of research whose real value lies in rescuing species that still survive. The mammoth, she says, is the advertisement, not the product.

Priya Nandakumar, an ecologist, is more interested in what the revived animals would do. She prefers to call them proxies: elephants edited to tolerate cold, for example, would not be mammoths but might still graze, trample snow and fertilise soil in ways that help to maintain Arctic grassland. For Nandakumar a proxy succeeds if it performs the ecological role of the lost species, and genetic identity is beside the point. She concedes, however, that a proxy would differ from the original in other ways. Much animal behaviour is learned from older generations, and with no surviving population to learn from, a revived creature would lack knowledge, such as migration routes or foraging techniques, that its ancestors once passed on.

Rafael Quintero, a philosopher of science, worries about the message such projects send. He calls the danger a moral hazard: if people come to believe that extinction can be reversed, they may feel less urgency about preventing it. Conservation budgets are finite, he notes, and public attention is finite too; a spectacular resurrection attracts donations and headlines that might otherwise have supported the protection of habitat. Quintero cites survey evidence suggesting that respondents who read an optimistic article about de-extinction were afterwards less supportive of protective legislation than those who did not. Supporters reply that the effect has not been shown to last, but Quintero maintains that a risk of this kind should be taken seriously before projects proceed.

A different argument is offered by David Achterberg, who contends that humans have a duty of repair. When our own actions have destroyed something of value, he argues, we are obliged to undo the damage where we can, just as a person who wrecks a neighbour's fence is expected to rebuild it. The duty is limited, however: it applies to species that people drove to extinction, such as the passenger pigeon, and not to those lost through natural causes. Quintero accepts the principle but doubts that it points towards resurrection, suggesting that the obligation is better discharged by protecting the species that remain. Achterberg answers that the two goals need not compete.

Concerns about animal welfare and ecological risk are raised by many critics. Because no artificial womb exists for large mammals, revived animals would have to be carried by surrogate mothers of related living species, a procedure that may cause suffering, and early attempts at cloning have produced many failed pregnancies. Once born, the animals would also pose questions about release. Ecologists warn that a reintroduced species might spread disease to existing wildlife, or outcompete native species for food and territory, as many introduced animals have done. Such risks are hard to predict, since the ecosystems that the animals once occupied have changed in their absence.

The geographer Mei-Lin Zhao draws attention to a group that is rarely consulted: the people who live in the landscapes where revived animals would be released. A thylacine returned to Tasmania, for instance, would share territory with farmers whose ancestors persecuted the animal, and with indigenous communities whose relationship with the land has its own history. Zhao argues that decisions are currently made in distant laboratories and funding bodies, and that the communities who would bear the consequences should help to determine whether, where and how any release takes place. Without such participation, she warns, even a technically successful project could be seen as an imposition.

Most commentators now accept that the question of whether we should bring species back is too blunt to be useful. A more productive approach is to ask under what conditions a particular project would be acceptable: whether the species was lost through human action, whether suitable habitat survives, whether the animals' welfare can be protected and whether affected communities consent. Judged in this way, some proposals may prove defensible and others not. The technology is advancing faster than the debate, however, and the absence of clear regulation means that decisions may be made by default rather than by deliberation.

title: Cooling the City: Urban Heat and the Politics of Planning
passage:
Cities have long been recognised as warmer than the countryside around them. The English chemist Luke Howard recorded the difference in London in the early nineteenth century, noting that the centre of the capital was consistently warmer than the surrounding fields, especially at night. Today the phenomenon, known as the urban heat island, has acquired new urgency. More than half of humanity lives in cities, and the proportion is rising, while climate change is making heatwaves longer and more intense. In dense districts, heat is no longer merely uncomfortable; it is a leading cause of weather-related death. Planners therefore face a pressing question: what, practically, can be done to cool the places where most people live?

Understanding the causes is a prerequisite for choosing remedies. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and tarred roofs absorb a large share of incoming solar radiation, while the replacement of soil and vegetation by pavement eliminates evaporative cooling, the process by which water leaving leaves and soil takes heat from the air. Tall buildings on narrow streets trap warmth and slow the wind, and engines and air-conditioning units add heat of their own. The climatologist Lucia Fernandes has shown that the contrast with rural areas is typically greatest not at midday but after sunset, because concrete and brick release stored heat slowly through the night. This matters for health, since the human body relies on cooler night hours to recover from daytime stress.

One widely promoted response is the reflective or cool roof. The engineer Sanjay Rao has demonstrated that coating a roof in light-coloured material, which reflects sunlight instead of absorbing it, can lower the temperature of the building beneath by several degrees at little cost. Applied across a district, the effect on air temperature can be significant. Critics raise objections. Light surfaces at street level can bounce radiation onto pedestrians, making them feel hotter; in cold seasons they may increase heating bills; and their reflectivity declines as dirt accumulates. Rao accepts these limitations but argues that newer coatings resist soiling and that roofs, unlike streets, are rarely walked upon.

Others place their faith in vegetation. The planner Oliver Bannister points out that trees cool in two ways, by casting shade and by releasing water vapour, and that a leafy street can be several degrees cooler than a bare one. His research suggests that the cooling effect of a park extends only a few hundred metres beyond its boundary. He concludes that a network of many small green spaces, scattered through a district, cools more of the city than a single large park of the same total area. Greening has its own difficulties, notably the need for water. In cities prone to drought, the irrigation required to keep trees alive may compete with household supplies.

Urban form is a further variable. Some European cities, notably Stuttgart, have protected corridors along which cool air from surrounding hills can flow into the centre, and have designed new buildings so as not to obstruct them. Yet ventilation conflicts with another planning goal. Compact, high-density development shortens journeys and so reduces emissions and waste heat from traffic, and it preserves farmland at the urban edge. At the same time, tall blocks packed closely together hinder airflow. Planners cannot simply abandon density; they must instead arrange it with care, leaving gaps and open routes through which air can move.

Heat is not shared equally. The social geographer Nomvula Dlamini has mapped temperatures across several cities and found that the hottest neighbourhoods are very often the poorest. They typically contain fewer trees and more paved surfaces, and their residents are less able to afford air conditioning. Dlamini warns, however, that cooling programmes may themselves create injustice. Once a district is made green and pleasant, property values rise, and the original residents may be priced out, so that the benefits flow to newcomers. She calls for measures, such as rent controls and community ownership of land, that protect existing residents as the environment improves.

The most common private response to heat, air conditioning, illustrates the difficulty of finding simple remedies. Air-conditioners cool interiors by expelling heat outdoors, and measurements in dense districts indicate that this can raise street temperatures noticeably, prompting still more people to install units. Mass use also drives up electricity demand, which in a heatwave can overload grids and cause blackouts, precisely when the vulnerable most need cooling. Fernandes describes this as a vicious circle: a technology adopted to escape the problem makes the problem worse for everyone, especially those who cannot afford it.

No single measure is likely to be sufficient. Reflective roofs, trees, ventilation corridors and social protections each address part of the problem, and the most effective strategies combine them according to local conditions. Such tailoring requires data, yet many cities, particularly in poorer countries, possess only a handful of temperature sensors, which leaves planners guessing about which districts are most at risk. The evidence available is nevertheless strong enough to justify action now. Waiting for perfect information would mean accepting further summers in which the heat falls hardest on the people least able to escape it.

title: The Making of Expertise
passage:
It is a familiar belief that mastery of any skill requires about ten thousand hours of practice. The idea is appealing because it promises that dedication, rather than inborn gifts, determines who becomes great. Scientific interest in expertise, however, began from a different question: what do experts actually do differently? In the mid-twentieth century, researchers studying chess masters expected to find that they simply calculated further ahead than weaker players. They found no such thing. Masters did not consider more moves, and often examined fewer. Their advantage lay in what they perceived in the instant they looked at a position, a finding that redirected the study of skill from the mechanics of reasoning to the structure of memory.

The psychologist Yusuf Demir has spent decades refining the explanation. Masters, he argues, do not see thirty-two pieces on a board; they see a smaller number of meaningful patterns, or chunks, built up through years of experience and stored in long-term memory. When shown a position from a real game for a few seconds, masters reconstruct it almost perfectly, while novices place only a handful of pieces. When the same pieces are arranged randomly, the masters' superiority largely vanishes, because the patterns that give them meaning are absent. Demir estimates that a master holds tens of thousands of such patterns, each linked to a sensible course of action, which allows good moves to come to mind without conscious search.

How such patterns are acquired is the subject of the theory of deliberate practice, associated with Karl Ostrander. Ostrander distinguishes it sharply from mere repetition. Deliberate practice consists of tasks designed to target a performer's particular weaknesses, carried out with full attention, accompanied by immediate feedback and usually guided by a teacher who can identify errors the learner cannot see. It is demanding, and by Ostrander's account performers can sustain it for only a few hours a day. In a well-known study of violin students, those judged the best had accumulated substantially more solitary practice by the age of twenty than their less accomplished peers. Hours alone, in other words, tell us little; what matters is what is done during them.

Ostrander's account has been challenged by the psychologist Fiona McAllister, who has examined dozens of studies of the relationship between practice and performance. She finds that practice explains a large share of the differences between performers in activities such as chess and music, but a much smaller share in fields such as teaching and the professions. Even within chess, she notes, individuals vary enormously in the amount of practice needed to reach master level. Two other factors repeatedly emerge from her analyses: the capacity of working memory, which allows some people to hold and manipulate more information at once, and the age at which training began. Ostrander replies that many of the studies define practice too loosely to capture the deliberate kind. The dispute therefore qualifies the theory rather than overturning it.

Expert intuition presents a further puzzle. The decision researcher Rosa Carvalho argues that intuition deserves trust only when two conditions are met: the environment must contain stable regularities, and the expert must have received prompt, clear feedback about past judgements. Chess players and firefighters work in such conditions, so their rapid judgements are often excellent. Stock-pickers and political forecasters do not; their environments are noisy and feedback is slow or ambiguous. Yet experience produces a feeling of certainty in either case, Carvalho observes, because the sense of knowing is generated by familiarity rather than by accuracy. A confident expert in an unforgiving environment may therefore be little more accurate than a simple rule of thumb.

Expertise also has costs. Because experts rely so heavily on stored patterns, they can be slow to cope when familiar conditions change. In experiments in which the conventions of a well-practised task were quietly altered, experts adjusted more slowly than people of moderate skill, who had less to unlearn. Experts may also struggle as teachers. Having forgotten what it was like not to know, they skip steps that seem obvious to them and bewilder beginners, a difficulty sometimes called the curse of knowledge. Demir suggests that the very efficiency of expert perception makes it hard for its owners to describe, since much of it operates below the level of awareness.

These findings have practical implications for education and training. Learners progress faster when practice is varied rather than repetitive, and when different types of problem are mixed together so that they must continually decide which method applies. Carvalho adds that trainees in unforgiving environments need feedback deliberately engineered for them, through simulations or systematic review of outcomes. There is also evidence that instructional methods must change as skill grows. Novices benefit from carefully worked examples that demonstrate each step, whereas the same examples can hinder more advanced learners, who learn better by tackling problems themselves, a phenomenon known as expertise reversal.

The old contest between talent and practice may therefore be a false opposition. Practice clearly matters, but so do memory capacity, starting age and the quality of teaching, and their relative weight differs from one domain to another. Expertise is not a single thing but a family of achievements, resting on different mechanisms in different settings. The most promising research, it seems, is no longer asking who is born to excel, but how particular kinds of experience reshape perception and memory, and under which conditions the resulting judgement can safely be trusted.
